mainTopic: Body and soul judged together, אנטונינוס's questions to רבי, contradictions about the future, proofs for תחיית המתים, and the sin of withholding Torah from a student.
overview: The amud opens at the end of רבי's parable to אנטונינוס. A lame guard and a blind guard teamed up to steal figs, so the owner judged them together. In the same way, God returns the נשמה to the גוף and judges them as one. אנטונינוס then asks רבי why the sun sets in the west, when the נשמה enters a person, and when the יצר הרע begins to rule. On the last two questions רבי accepts אנטונינוס's view and supports it with a פסוק. Next comes a series of contradictions between פסוקים about the future, raised by ריש לקיש, עולא, רב חסדא and רבא, and each one is resolved. A ברייתא and several אמוראים then bring proofs for תחיית המתים, mostly from future-tense verbs like יָשִׁיר and יְהַלְלוּךָ. The amud ends with teachings on how serious it is to hold back הלכה from a student, and the last proof פסוק continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The lame guard and the blind guard steal the figs
steps.stepSummary: Continuing his parable, רבי describes an orchard with fine early figs and two guards, one lame and one blind. Working together, they steal and eat the fruit.
steps.simpleTranslation: The orchard had fine early figs, and the owner placed two guards in it: one lame and one blind. The lame one said to the blind one, 'I see fine early figs in the orchard. Come, carry me, and we'll bring them and eat them.' The lame man rode on the blind man's back, and they brought the figs and ate them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is in the middle of רבי's answer to אנטונינוס. This line tells the first half of his parable, where the two guards team up to steal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Neither guard could steal alone. The lame one can see but cannot walk, and the blind one can walk but cannot see. This sets up the point that body and soul each sin only by working together.
steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new story. It is the middle of רבי's parable answering אנטונינוס's claim that body and soul can each escape judgment.

phrases.english: fine first fruits (early figs),
and he placed two guards in it:
one lame and one blind.
The lame one said to the blind one:
I see fine first fruits in the orchard.
Come, carry me, and we will bring them to eat them.
The lame one rode on the back of the blind one,
and they brought them and ate them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues רבי's parable, which began before this section.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The first half of the parable: the two guards can only steal by teaming up.

steps.title: Each guard makes an excuse, and the owner judges them together
steps.stepSummary: The owner asks where the figs went. Each guard claims his disability made the theft impossible, so the owner puts the lame one back on the blind one and judges them as one.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some time later the orchard owner came and asked them, 'Where are the fine early figs?' The lame one said, 'Do I have legs to walk with?' The blind one said, 'Do I have eyes to see with?' What did the owner do? He put the lame man on the blind man's back and judged them together.
steps.whatsHappening: The parable reaches its climax. Each guard tries to escape blame by himself, and the owner answers by judging them as the team they were when they stole.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each excuse is true only if the guard is considered alone. The owner rebuilds the exact partnership that committed the theft. Judging them together closes the loophole each one tried to use.

keyTerms.meaning: Do I have anything at all? (a rhetorical 'nothing')

phrases.english: Some time later, the owner of the orchard came.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לָהֶן: בַּכּוּרוֹת נָאוֹת הֵיכָן הֵן?
phrases.english: He said to them: The fine first fruits, where are they?
The lame one said to him:

phrases.aramaic: כְּלוּם יֵשׁ לִי רַגְלַיִם לְהַלֵּךְ בָּהֶן?
phrases.english: Do I have any legs to walk with?
The blind one said to him:
Do I have any eyes to see with?
What did he do?
He placed the lame one on the back of the blind one,
and judged them as one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the parable begun in step 1.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Partners who sin together cannot each escape by blaming their own limits. They are judged together.

steps.title: So too, God returns the soul to the body and judges them together
steps.stepSummary: רבי applies the parable: הקדוש ברוך הוא puts the נשמה back into the גוף and judges them as one. He proves this from a פסוק in which 'the heavens' is the נשמה and 'the earth' is the גוף.
steps.simpleTranslation: So too, the Holy One, Blessed be He, brings the soul, throws it back into the body, and judges them as one. As it says: 'He calls to the heavens above, and to the earth, to judge His people.' 'He calls to the heavens above' refers to the soul. 'And to the earth, to judge His people' refers to the body.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי applies his parable to the real question and finishes his answer to אנטונינוס. Body and soul are judged together, and he backs this up with a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The lame man who can see matches the נשמה, and the blind man who can walk matches the גוף. Just as the owner rejoined the two guards, God rejoins נשמה and גוף. The פסוק calls on both heaven and earth for judgment, which shows that both parts are judged together.

keyTerms.meaning: As it is stated (introduces a פסוק)

steps.whatToRemember: A person is judged as a whole. The נשמה and the גוף sinned together, so הקדוש ברוך הוא reunites them and judges them together, just like the lame and blind guards.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is רבי's full answer to אנטונינוס's challenge that neither body nor soul could be held responsible on its own.

phrases.english: So too, the Holy One, Blessed be He,
brings the soul and throws it into the body,
and judges them as one,
as it is stated: 'He calls to the heavens above
phrases.notes: תהלים 50:4

phrases.english: and to the earth, to judge His people.'
'He calls to the heavens above': this is the soul,
'and to the earth, to judge His people': this is the body.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַף הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מֵבִיא נְשָׁמָה וְזוֹרְקָהּ בַּגּוּף
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the parable to body and soul and adds a supporting פסוק.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Body and soul are reunited and judged together.

steps.title: Why does the sun rise in the east and set in the west?
steps.stepSummary: A new exchange begins: אנטונינוס asks רבי why the sun rises in the east and sets in the west.
steps.simpleTranslation: אנטונינוס said to רבי: Why does the sun come out in the east and set in the west?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a brand-new conversation between אנטונינוס and רבי. This question sets up the next moves.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This topic has nothing to do with the body-and-soul discussion. The question as asked is very broad, and רבי will challenge that in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: A Roman ruler who was friendly with רבי

phrases.english: Antoninus said to Rabbi:
Why does the sun come out in the east
and set in the west?

steps.triggerLanguage: מִפְּנֵי מָה חַמָּה יוֹצְאָה בַּמִּזְרָח וְשׁוֹקַעַת בְּמַעֲרָב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new, unrelated exchange.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason the sun rises in the east and sets in the west.

steps.title: רבי: you would ask the same question either way
steps.stepSummary: רבי points out that if the sun moved the opposite way, אנטונינוס would ask the same question. So the question, as phrased, does not really ask anything.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי said to him: If it were the reverse, you would have asked me the same thing.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי pushes back on the question itself instead of answering it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The sun has to rise on one side and set on the other. Asking 'why this way and not the reverse' has no real answer, because the reverse would raise the same question. אנטונינוס will need to sharpen what he is asking.

phrases.english: He said to him:
If it were the reverse,
you would also have said this to me.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הֲוָה אִיפְּכָא נָמֵי הָכִי הֲוָה אָמְרַתְּ לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the way the question in step 4 was framed.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The wording of אנטונינוס's question as a whole.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The question would apply equally to the opposite case, so as asked it has no real content.

steps.title: אנטונינוס sharpens his question: why set in the west?
steps.stepSummary: אנטונינוס clarifies that he is really asking why the sun sets specifically in the west.
steps.simpleTranslation: אנטונינוס said to him: This is what I am asking you: why does it set in the west?
steps.whatsHappening: אנטונינוס restates his question in a narrower form. The next step gives רבי's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He drops the 'east versus west' comparison that רבי rejected. He now focuses only on why the sun goes down in the west. This sets up רבי's answer next.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what I am saying to you

phrases.english: He said to him: This is what I am saying to you:
Why does it set in the west?

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכִי קָאָמֵינָא לָךְ מִפְּנֵי מָה שׁוֹקַעַת בַּמַּעֲרָב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Reframes the question after רבי's pushback in step 5.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The specific reason the sun sets in the west.

steps.title: The sun sets in the west to bow to its Creator
steps.stepSummary: רבי answers that the sun sets in the west to greet its Creator, based on a פסוק that the heavenly hosts bow to God.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: To greet its Owner, as the פסוק says, 'And the hosts of heaven bow down to You.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי answers אנטונינוס's question from the step before: the sun sets in the west to give 'שלום' to its Creator.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The sun's setting is treated like an act of bowing to God. The פסוק shows that the heavenly bodies, including the sun, bow to God. So the sun's daily path ends with a kind of greeting to Him.

keyTerms.meaning: its Owner, meaning its Creator, God
to give greeting, to pay respects
the hosts of heaven (sun, moon, stars)

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: כְּדֵי לִיתֵּן שָׁלוֹם לְקוֹנָהּ,
phrases.english: He said to him: In order to greet its Owner,
as it is said: 'And the hosts of heaven bow down to You.'
phrases.notes: נחמיה 9:6

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: כְּדֵי לִיתֵּן שָׁלוֹם לְקוֹנָהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the clarified question from step 6.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why does the sun set specifically in the west?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: To greet its Creator by bowing, as the heavenly hosts bow to God.

steps.title: Why not bow at mid-sky and go back?
steps.stepSummary: אנטונינוס challenges: let the sun go up to the middle of the sky, bow there, and go back the way it came.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Then let it come up to the middle of the sky, give its greeting, and go back in!
steps.whatsHappening: אנטונינוס pushes back on רבי's answer. If the point is only to greet God, the sun doesn't need to travel all the way to the west.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge says the reason given is not enough to explain the whole path. A greeting could happen halfway, and then the sun could return east. So something else must explain why it keeps going all the way west.

keyTerms.meaning: and let it go in, meaning go back

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: וְתֵיתֵי עַד פַּלְגָא דְרָקִיעַ,
phrases.english: He said to him: Then let it come up to the middle of the sky,
and give its greeting, and go back in!
phrases.notes: He means: go back to where it started in the east and set there.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: וְתֵיתֵי עַד פַּלְגָא דְרָקִיעַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in step 7.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי's reason that the sun goes west to greet its Creator.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A greeting could be done at mid-sky, so the reason does not explain why the sun travels the full distance to the west.

steps.title: For the sake of workers and travelers
steps.stepSummary: רבי answers that the sun keeps going west for the sake of workers and travelers.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because of workers, and because of travelers on the roads.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי gives a second reason: the sun's full path from east to west helps workers and travelers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The greeting explains the direction, and this reason explains the full journey. People who work or travel need the day to move steadily across the sky so they can plan their time.
steps.whatToRemember: The sun goes west to bow to its Creator. It travels the whole way across the sky for the sake of workers and travelers.

phrases.english: Because of workers and because of travelers.
phrases.notes: The words 'he said to him' are left out here, but this is רבי answering.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 8.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The sun could greet God at mid-sky and turn back.
steps.terutzMaskana: It keeps going west so workers and travelers can rely on the day's steady course.

steps.title: When does the soul enter a person?
steps.stepSummary: אנטונינוס asks רבי whether the נשמה is given at conception or when the embryo takes shape.
steps.simpleTranslation: And אנטונינוס said to רבי: From when is the soul placed in a person: from conception, or from when the body is formed?
steps.whatsHappening: A new question begins. אנטונינוס asks at what stage the נשמה enters a person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He offers two choices. פקידה is the very start, at conception. יצירה is a later stage, when the embryo takes form.

phrases.english: And Antoninos said to Rabbi:
From when is the soul placed in a person:
from the time of conception or from the time of formation?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר לוֹ אַנְטוֹנִינוּס לְרַבִּי: נְשָׁמָה מֵאֵימָתַי נִיתְּנָה בָּאָדָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new conversation topic.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: At what stage the soul enters a person: conception or formation.

steps.title: רבי says: at formation
steps.stepSummary: רבי answers that the נשמה enters when the embryo is formed.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: From the time of formation.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי gives his first answer: the נשמה comes at יצירה. This sets up אנטונינוס's challenge in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי picks the later of the two choices. The גמרא records this first answer so it can show how רבי changed his mind after אנטונינוס's challenge.

phrases.english: He said to him: From the time of formation.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 10.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The soul is given at formation.

steps.title: Meat without salt would rot
steps.stepSummary: אנטונינוס argues that flesh cannot last without a נשמה, just as meat rots within three days without salt, so the נשמה must come at conception.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Is it possible for a piece of meat to last three days without salt and not rot? Rather, it must be from conception.
steps.whatsHappening: אנטונינוס challenges רבי's answer with an example from everyday life and suggests the other option.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Meat without salt spoils in a few days. An embryo with no נשמה would be like that meat and could not survive until יצירה. So the נשמה must already be there from פקידה, acting like the 'salt' that keeps it alive.

keyTerms.meaning: salt, used to keep meat from spoiling

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לוֹ: אֶפְשָׁר חֲתִיכָה שֶׁל בָּשָׂר
phrases.english: He said to him: Is it possible that a piece of meat
can stand three days without salt
and not rot?
Rather, it is from the time of conception.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לוֹ: אֶפְשָׁר חֲתִיכָה שֶׁל בָּשָׂר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי's answer in step 11 and offers the other option.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי's answer that the soul comes at formation.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Flesh without a preserving force rots quickly, so an embryo could not survive without a soul until formation.

steps.title: רבי agrees and brings a פסוק
steps.stepSummary: רבי admits he learned this from אנטונינוס and supports it with a פסוק using the word פקודתך.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי said: אנטונינוס taught me this, and a פסוק supports him: 'And Your פקודה guarded my spirit.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי accepts אנטונינוס's view and shows that a פסוק backs it up.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says God's פקודה guarded 'my spirit.' The word פקודתך sounds like פקידה, so it shows the spirit is there from conception.

keyTerms.meaning: Your פקודה (linked here to פקידה, conception)

steps.whatToRemember: The נשמה enters at conception (פקידה), not later at formation.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי: דָּבָר זֶה לִמְּדַנִי אַנְטוֹנִינוּס,
phrases.english: Rabbi said: Antoninos taught me this thing,
and a verse supports him, as it is said:
'And Your providence guarded my spirit.'
phrases.notes: איוב 10:12. The word פקודתך is being read as connected to פקידה, conception.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי: דָּבָר זֶה לִמְּדַנִי אַנְטוֹנִינוּס, וּמִקְרָא מְסַיְּיעוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts the challenge of step 12 and supports it with a פסוק.
steps.raayaObject: The soul is given at conception.

steps.title: When does the יצר הרע begin to rule?
steps.stepSummary: אנטונינוס asks whether the יצר הרע controls a person from formation or from birth.
steps.simpleTranslation: And אנטונינוס said to רבי: From when does the יצר הרע rule over a person: from formation, or from leaving the womb?
steps.whatsHappening: Another new question begins, this time about when the יצר הרע starts to rule a person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Again there are two choices. יצירה is in the womb. יציאה is birth, when the baby comes out.

phrases.english: And Antoninos said to Rabbi:
From when does the evil inclination rule over a person:
from the time of formation or from the time of coming out?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר לוֹ אַנְטוֹנִינוּס לְרַבִּי: מֵאֵימָתַי יֵצֶר הָרָע שׁוֹלֵט בָּאָדָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new question with the same pattern as step 10.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: When the evil inclination begins to rule: formation or birth.

steps.title: רבי says: at formation
steps.stepSummary: רבי answers that the יצר הרע rules from formation.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: From the time of formation.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי gives his first answer, and it sets up אנטונינוס's challenge in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Just like before, רבי picks יצירה. The pattern of answer, challenge, and agreement is about to repeat.

phrases.english: He said to him: From the time of formation.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 14.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The evil inclination rules from formation.

steps.title: The baby would kick its way out
steps.stepSummary: אנטונינוס argues that if the יצר הרע ruled in the womb, the baby would kick its mother and push out early, so it must start at birth.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: If so, it would kick in its mother's womb and come out! Rather, it is from birth.
steps.whatsHappening: אנטונינוס challenges רבי's answer and suggests the other option.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A baby controlled by the יצר הרע would act wildly and harm its mother. Since babies stay calmly in the womb until birth, the יצר הרע must start only at יציאה.

phrases.english: He said to him: If so,
it would kick in its mother's womb and come out!
Rather, it is from the time of coming out.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לוֹ: אִם כֵּן, בּוֹעֵט בִּמְעֵי אִמּוֹ וְיוֹצֵא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי's answer in step 15.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי's answer that the evil inclination rules from formation.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: An embryo ruled by the evil inclination would kick and force its way out, which does not happen.

steps.title: Sin crouches at the opening
steps.stepSummary: רבי agrees and supports it with the פסוק 'לפתח חטאת רובץ'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי said: אנטונינוס taught me this, and a פסוק supports him: 'Sin crouches at the opening.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי accepts אנטונינוס's view again and brings a פסוק that supports it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'opening' is read as the opening of the womb. So sin, meaning the יצר הרע, waits for a person right at birth.
steps.whatToRemember: The יצר הרע begins to rule a person at birth (יציאה), not in the womb.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי: דָּבָר זֶה לִמְּדַנִי אַנְטוֹנִינוּס,
phrases.english: Rabbi said: Antoninos taught me this thing,
and a verse supports him, as it is said:
'Sin crouches at the opening.'
phrases.notes: בראשית 4:7. The 'opening' is read as the opening of the womb, meaning birth.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי: דָּבָר זֶה לִמְּדַנִי אַנְטוֹנִינוּס, וּמִקְרָא מְסַיְּיעוֹ, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts the challenge of step 16 and supports it with a פסוק.
steps.raayaObject: The evil inclination begins to rule at birth.

steps.title: Two פסוקים clash about the blind and the lame
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש points out a contradiction: one פסוק says the blind and lame will be among those brought back, while another says the lame will leap and the mute will sing.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש pointed out a contradiction: It is written, 'With them the blind and the lame, the pregnant woman and the one giving birth together,' and it is written, 'Then the lame will leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute will sing, for water will burst out in the desert and streams in the wilderness.'
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic begins. ריש לקיש sets two פסוקים next to each other that seem to disagree about the future.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first פסוק says people will come back still blind and lame. The second says the lame will leap and the mute will sing, meaning they are healed. Both cannot be true at the same moment.

keyTerms.meaning: points out a contradiction (literally, 'throws' two sources against each other)

phrases.english: Reish Lakish pointed out a contradiction:
It is written: 'With them the blind and the lame,
the pregnant woman and the one giving birth together,'
phrases.notes: ירמיהו 31:7

phrases.english: and it is written: 'Then the lame will leap like a deer,
and the tongue of the mute will sing,
for water will burst out in the desert,
and streams in the wilderness.'
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 35:6

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, unrelated to the אנטונינוס conversations.
steps.kashyaTarget: The two פסוקים about people with defects in the future.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: One פסוק has them still blind and lame, and the other has them healed. These seem to contradict.

steps.title: They rise with their defects, then are healed
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש resolves it: people rise with their defects and are then healed.
steps.simpleTranslation: How so? They rise with their defects, and then they are healed.
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש solves his own contradiction by putting the two פסוקים at two different stages.
steps.deeperAnalysis: First people come back exactly as they were, defects and all, which fits ירמיהו. Afterward they are healed, which fits ישעיהו. Each פסוק describes a different moment.

keyTerms.meaning: how so? how do these fit together?

steps.whatToRemember: There is no contradiction. People rise with their defects first, and are healed afterward.

phrases.english: How so?
They rise with their defects, and then they are healed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the contradiction of step 18.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוקים seem to describe the same moment, so they clash.
steps.terutzMaskana: First they rise with their defects (ירמיהו), then they are healed (ישעיהו).

steps.title: עולא's contradiction: will there be death in the future or not?
steps.stepSummary: עולא points out that one פסוק says death will be swallowed forever, while another says people will die at a hundred.
steps.simpleTranslation: עולא raises a contradiction. One פסוק says: 'He will swallow death forever, and ה׳ will wipe tears from all faces.' Another פסוק says: 'For the youth shall die a hundred years old; there shall no longer be from there an infant of few days.'
steps.whatsHappening: עולא sets two פסוקים in ישעיהו side by side because they seem to disagree about whether people will die in the future.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first פסוק says death will be gone completely. The second still talks about people dying, just at an old age. Both cannot be describing the same people in the same way.

keyTerms.meaning: Raises a contradiction (literally 'throws' two sources against each other)
An infant only a few days old

phrases.english: Ulla raises a contradiction:
It is written: "He will swallow death forever

phrases.aramaic: וּמָחָה ה׳ דִּמְעָה מֵעַל כׇּל פָּנִים״,
phrases.english: and ה׳ will wipe tears from all faces,"
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 25:8

phrases.aramaic: וּכְתִיב ״כִּי הַנַּעַר בֶּן מֵאָה שָׁנָה יָמוּת
phrases.english: And it is written: "For the youth shall die a hundred years old

phrases.aramaic: לֹא יִהְיֶה מִשָּׁם עוֹד עוּל יָמִים״.
phrases.english: there shall no longer be from there an infant of few days."
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 65:20. So people still die here, just very old.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows the same pattern as ריש לקיש's contradiction in step 18: two פסוקים about the future that seem to clash.
steps.kashyaTarget: The two פסוקים in ישעיהו about death in the future
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: One פסוק says death ends forever, and the other says people will still die at a hundred. These look like opposite pictures.

steps.title: One פסוק is about ישראל, the other about אומות העולם
steps.stepSummary: The contradiction is resolved: the end of death applies to ישראל, and dying at a hundred applies to אומות העולם.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. Here it speaks of the Jewish people, and there it speaks of the nations of the world.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers עולא by saying the two פסוקים are about two different groups of people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Death being swallowed forever is about ישראל, who will live forever. Dying at a hundred is about אומות העולם, who will live very long lives but still die. So both פסוקים are true.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult; this is how the גמרא opens an answer
Here... there; each source is about a different case
The nations of the world, meaning non-Jews

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
Here, regarding the Jewish people,
phrases.notes: This is the פסוק about death being swallowed forever.

phrases.english: there, regarding the nations of the world.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers עולא's contradiction.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases: each פסוק is about a different group of people.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both פסוקים describe the same people, so they clash.
steps.terutzMaskana: Death ends forever for ישראל, while אומות העולם live very long but still die.

steps.title: Why would the nations be there at all?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why אומות העולם would be present in that future time.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the nations of the world, what are they doing there?
steps.whatsHappening: The answer in step 21 raises a new question: why would the nations even be alive in that future time? The גמרא asks this and then answers it in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 21 assumed that אומות העולם live in that future time. The גמרא wants to know what role they have there.

keyTerms.meaning: What are they doing there? (literally 'what do they want there?')

phrases.english: And the nations of the world,
what are they doing there?
phrases.notes: "There" means in that future time when death is swallowed up.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about an assumption hidden inside the answer of step 21.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What role אומות העולם will have in the future time.

steps.title: They are the nations who will serve as farmers and shepherds
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers with a פסוק: these are the foreigners who will tend the flocks and fields of ישראל.
steps.simpleTranslation: These are the ones about whom it is written: 'And strangers shall stand and feed your flocks, and foreigners shall be your plowmen and your vinedressers.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 22 with a פסוק that gives the nations a job in the future.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק describes foreigners working the flocks, fields and vineyards of ישראל. This explains why some of אומות העולם will be present then.

keyTerms.meaning: Your plowmen and your vineyard workers

steps.whatToRemember: עולא's contradiction is solved by splitting the groups: for ישראל death ends forever, and the nations who serve them will live long lives but still die.

phrases.english: Those about whom it is written:
"And strangers shall stand and feed your flocks,
and foreigners shall be your plowmen and your vinedressers."
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 61:5

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 22.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The nations who are there are the ones who will work as shepherds and farmers for ישראל, as the פסוק describes.

steps.title: רב חסדא's contradiction: will the sun and moon fade or shine brighter?
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא points out that one פסוק says the sun and moon will be ashamed, while another says they will shine much brighter.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא raises a contradiction. One פסוק says: 'The moon shall be confounded and the sun ashamed, for ה׳ of hosts will reign.' Another says: 'The light of the moon shall be like the light of the sun, and the light of the sun shall be sevenfold, like the light of the seven days.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא brings a new pair of פסוקים in ישעיהו that seem to disagree about the sun and moon in the future.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One פסוק makes the sun and moon look dim and 'ashamed' when God reigns. The other says they will shine far more strongly than now. These look like opposite pictures.

keyTerms.meaning: The moon will be confounded, as if embarrassed and dimmed
And the sun will be ashamed

phrases.english: Rav Chisda raises a contradiction:
It is written: "Then the moon shall be confounded and the sun ashamed,
for ה׳ of hosts will reign,"
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 24:23

phrases.english: And it is written: "And the light of the moon shall be like the light of the sun,
and the light of the sun shall be sevenfold,
like the light of the seven days."
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 30:26

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new contradiction in the same series of contradictions about the future.
steps.kashyaTarget: The two פסוקים in ישעיהו about the sun and moon in the future
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: One פסוק says they will be dimmed and ashamed, and the other says they will shine seven times brighter.

steps.title: One פסוק is about ימות המשיח, the other about עולם הבא
steps.stepSummary: The brighter sun and moon belong to ימות המשיח, and the 'ashamed' sun and moon belong to עולם הבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. Here it speaks of the days of the Messiah, and there it speaks of the World to Come.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers רב חסדא by saying the two פסוקים describe two different future time periods.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In ימות המשיח the sun and moon will shine more strongly. In עולם הבא they will look dim, because the main light will be God's own light. So each פסוק fits a different era.

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
Here, regarding the days of the Messiah,
phrases.notes: This is the פסוק where the sun and moon shine brighter.

phrases.english: there, regarding the World to Come.
phrases.notes: This is the פסוק where the sun and moon are "ashamed."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב חסדא's contradiction.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the time periods: each פסוק is about a different era.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both פסוקים describe the same future time, so they clash.
steps.terutzMaskana: The sun and moon shine brighter in ימות המשיח and look dim in עולם הבא.

steps.title: But שמואל says ימות המשיח brings no change in nature
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how שמואל would answer, since he holds that ימות המשיח differs from today only in freedom from the exile.
steps.simpleTranslation: And according to שמואל, who said: 'The only difference between this world and the days of the Messiah is the subjugation of the exiles.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer of step 25 using שמואל's view. This line sets up the question, and the next step gives the answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 25 said the sun and moon will shine brighter in ימות המשיח. But שמואל holds that in ימות המשיח nature stays the same, and the only change is that ישראל will be free from foreign rule. So according to שמואל, step 25's answer does not work.

keyTerms.meaning: The subjugation of the exiles, being ruled by other nations

phrases.english: And according to Shmuel, who said:
phrases.notes: The question is left unsaid: how would שמואל answer רב חסדא's contradiction?

phrases.aramaic: אֵין בֵּין הָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה לִימוֹת הַמָּשִׁיחַ
phrases.english: There is no difference between this world and the days of the Messiah
except the subjugation of the exiles alone,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer in step 25 using שמואל's opinion.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that the brighter light belongs to ימות המשיח
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: שמואל holds that nature will not change in ימות המשיח, so the sun cannot become seven times brighter then.

steps.title: For שמואל: the camp of the righteous versus the camp of the שכינה
steps.stepSummary: According to שמואל, the two פסוקים describe two different 'camps' rather than two different eras.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. Here it speaks of the camp of the righteous, and there it speaks of the camp of the שכינה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a different answer that works even for שמואל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of splitting by time period, this answer splits by place. In the camp of the righteous the sun and moon shine brighter. In the camp of the שכינה they look dim next to God's light.

keyTerms.meaning: The camp of the Divine Presence

steps.whatToRemember: רב חסדא's contradiction has two answers: different eras (ימות המשיח and עולם הבא), or, for שמואל, different 'camps' (the righteous and the שכינה).

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
Here, in the camp of the righteous,
phrases.notes: This matches the פסוק about brighter light.

phrases.english: there, in the camp of the Divine Presence.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the problem of step 26 with a new way to split the פסוקים.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting by place instead of by time.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Without ימות המשיח as an answer, the two פסוקים seem to clash again.
steps.terutzMaskana: Brighter light belongs to the camp of the righteous, and the dimmed sun and moon belong to the camp of the שכינה.

steps.title: רבא's contradiction: bringing to life versus healing
steps.stepSummary: רבא contrasts 'I kill and I bring to life' with 'I wounded and I will heal'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא raises a contradiction. It is written: 'I kill and I bring to life.' And it is written: 'I wounded and I will heal.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא points out two phrases from the same פסוק that seem to say different things about what God does.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first phrase says God brings the dead back to life. The second phrase speaks only of healing wounds. It is unclear which one describes what God will do.

keyTerms.meaning: I kill and I bring to life
I wounded and I will heal

phrases.english: Rava raises a contradiction:
It is written: "I kill and I bring to life,"
phrases.notes: דברים 32:39

phrases.english: And it is written: "I wounded and I will heal."
phrases.notes: These words come right after, in the same פסוק.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new contradiction in the series, now about תחיית המתים.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: One half speaks of reviving the dead and the other only of healing the wounded, so it is unclear what God's action will be.

steps.title: First God revives, then God heals
steps.stepSummary: הקדוש ברוך הוא says: whoever I killed I bring back to life, and after that, whoever I wounded I heal.
steps.simpleTranslation: הקדוש ברוך הוא said: 'Whoever I put to death, I bring to life. And then, whoever I wounded, I will heal.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers רבא by reading the two phrases as two stages, one after the other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrases do not clash, because they describe a sequence. First the dead are brought back to life, and then ("והדר") their wounds are healed. This fits the idea in step 19 that people rise with their defects and are then healed.

keyTerms.meaning: The Holy One, Blessed be He
Puts to death... brings to life

steps.whatToRemember: רבא's two phrases are two stages: first תחיית המתים, then healing.

phrases.english: The Holy One, Blessed be He, said:
What I put to death, I bring to life,
and then, what I wounded, I will heal.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא: מַה שֶּׁאֲנִי מֵמִית – אֲנִי מְחַיֶּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבא's contradiction.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reading the two phrases as a sequence rather than as competing descriptions.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק gives two different, clashing pictures of what God does.
steps.terutzMaskana: God first brings the dead back to life and afterward heals their wounds.

steps.title: Maybe one person dies and a different person lives
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא raises the possibility that 'I kill and I bring to life' means death for one person and birth for another, as happens in normal life.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages taught: 'I kill and I bring to life.' You might think this means one person dies and a different person is given life, the way the world normally works.
steps.whatsHappening: A ברייתא brings up a possible wrong reading of the פסוק 'I kill and I bring to life.' It is setting up the answer that comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The simple reading could be about the normal cycle of life: some people die and other people are born. If that were the meaning, the פסוק would teach nothing about תחיית המתים.

keyTerms.meaning: I kill and I bring to life
One might think (introduces a possible but wrong idea)
The way the world normally works

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
"I kill and I bring to life"
phrases.notes: דברים 32:39. This is the same פסוק רבא used in step 28.

phrases.english: One might think that there will be death for one person
and life for another person,
the way the world normally works?

steps.triggerLanguage: יָכוֹל שֶׁתְּהֵא מִיתָה בְּאֶחָד וְחַיִּים בְּאֶחָד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a ברייתא on the same פסוק that רבא discussed in steps 28-29.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does 'I kill and I bring to life' describe different people, or the same person?

steps.title: Like wounding and healing, death and life happen to the same person
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא proves from 'I wounded and I will heal' that the one who dies is the same one who comes back to life, which answers those who deny that תחיית המתים is in the תורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: The verse says: 'I wounded and I will heal.' Just as wounding and healing happen to one person, so too death and life happen to one person. From here we can answer those who say תחיית המתים is not in the תורה.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא rejects the 'different people' reading by pointing to the second half of the פסוק. It then concludes that this is a proof of תחיית המתים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Healing only makes sense for the same person who was wounded. Since both halves of the פסוק belong together, 'I kill and I bring to life' must also be about one person who dies and then lives again. That is תחיית המתים.

keyTerms.meaning: The verse comes to teach (introduces the proof)
I wounded and I will heal
The dead coming back to life
An answer or reply (here, against the deniers)

steps.whatToRemember: Death and life in this פסוק happen to the same person, just like wounding and healing do. That makes it a source in the תורה for תחיית המתים.

phrases.english: The verse teaches: "I wounded and I will heal"
just as wounding and healing happen to one person,
so too, death and life happen to one person.
From here there is an answer to those who say
that there is no resurrection of the dead from the Torah.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the possible reading raised in step 30.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The same person dies and is brought back to life, as shown by the comparison to wounding and healing.

steps.title: רבי מאיר: 'Then משה will sing' is in the future tense
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר proves תחיית המתים from the future-tense word 'will sing' in אז ישיר.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי מאיר said: Where does the תורה show תחיית המתים? It says: 'Then משה and the children of Israel will sing this song to ה׳.' It does not say 'sang,' but 'will sing.' From here we learn תחיית המתים from the תורה.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי מאיר brings a new proof for תחיית המתים, built on the exact tense of a word in the פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The song at the sea already happened, so you would expect the past tense 'sang.' Because the פסוק says 'will sing,' רבי מאיר reads it as a hint that משה will sing again in the future, which means he will come back to life.

keyTerms.meaning: It does not say... but rather... (points to an exact word choice)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two words: שָׁר means 'sang' (past) and יָשִׁיר means 'will sing' (future). The whole proof depends on that difference.

phrases.english: It was taught: Rabbi Meir said:
From where is resurrection of the dead derived from the Torah?
As it is stated: "Then Moshe and the children of Israel will sing
this song to ה׳."
phrases.notes: שמות 15:1

phrases.english: It does not say "sang," but rather "will sing"
From here we learn resurrection of the dead from the Torah.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new, separate proof for תחיית המתים, using a different method.
steps.raayaObject: תחיית המתים is found in the תורה.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The future tense יָשִׁיר in שמות 15:1.

steps.title: Same idea: 'Then יהושע will build'
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר adds a parallel example: 'Then יהושע will build an altar' also uses the future tense.
steps.simpleTranslation: In the same way, you can say: 'Then יהושע will build an altar to ה׳.' It does not say 'built,' but 'will build.' From here we learn תחיית המתים from the תורה.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי מאיר shows that the same future-tense pattern appears in another פסוק, which supports his method.
steps.deeperAnalysis: יהושע built the altar long ago, yet the פסוק says 'will build.' Like with משה, the future tense hints that he will live again. A second example makes the method look like a real pattern and not a one-time oddity.

phrases.english: Similarly, you can say:
"Then Yehoshua will build an altar to ה׳."
phrases.notes: יהושע 8:30

phrases.english: It does not say "built," but rather "will build"
From here we learn resurrection of the dead from the Torah.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second example of רבי מאיר's future-tense proof.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The future tense יִבְנֶה in יהושע 8:30.

steps.title: Challenge: will שלמה build an idol's altar in the future?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the future-tense method: a פסוק says 'Then שלמה will build a במה for כמוש,' and surely that does not mean he will do it again.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if so, what about 'Then שלמה will build a במה for כמוש, the abomination of מואב'? Does that also mean he will build it in the future?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רבי מאיר's method by bringing a פסוק where reading the future tense literally gives a bad result.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If every future-tense 'אז יבנה' means a future event, then שלמה would come back to life to build an altar for idol worship. That cannot be right. So the future tense alone may not prove anything.

keyTerms.meaning: But if so... (introduces a challenge from your own logic)
An altar or raised place for offerings
So too? (here, asking if the same reading applies)

phrases.english: But if so,
"Then Shlomo will build an altar
for Kemosh, the abomination of Moav"
phrases.notes: מלכים א 11:7

phrases.english: does it also mean that he will build it in the future?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the method used in steps 32-33.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי מאיר's rule that a future-tense verb hints at תחיית המתים.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same rule applied to the שלמה פסוק would mean he will build an idol's altar in the future, which is absurd.

steps.title: The פסוק counts it against שלמה as if he built it
steps.stepSummary: The future tense in the שלמה פסוק has a different explanation: the פסוק treats him as though he built it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the פסוק considers it as if he built it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the שלמה פסוק differently, so it no longer works as a challenge to רבי מאיר's proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the שלמה פסוק, the unusual wording teaches that he is held responsible as if he built it, even though he did not really build it. That special explanation applies only there, so the proofs from משה and יהושע still stand.

keyTerms.meaning: The פסוק considers him; counts it against him

phrases.english: Rather, the verse counts it against him
phrases.notes: The גמרא means שלמה did not really build it himself.

phrases.english: as if he built it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא מַעֲלֶה עָלָיו הַכָּתוּב כְּאִילּוּ בָּנָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 34.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives the problem פסוק its own separate explanation.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Every future-tense 'אז יבנה' must mean a real future event, including שלמה's.
steps.terutzMaskana: The שלמה פסוק means he is considered as if he built it; this does not weaken the proofs from משה and יהושע.

steps.title: רבי יהושע בן לוי: 'They will yet praise You'
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע בן לוי proves תחיית המתים from the future-tense 'יהללוך' in תהלים.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהושע בן לוי said: Where do we find תחיית המתים in the תורה? It says: 'Happy are those who dwell in Your house; they will yet praise You, סלה.' It does not say 'they praised You,' but 'they will praise You.' From here we learn תחיית המתים.
steps.whatsHappening: Another אמורא gives a new future-tense proof for תחיית המתים, this time from תהלים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'will yet praise' point to praise that continues in the future, even for people who already lived. As with רבי מאיר, the future tense is read as a hint that they will live again.

keyTerms.meaning: Happy are those who dwell in Your house

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said:
From where is resurrection of the dead derived from the Torah?
As it is stated: "Happy are those who dwell in Your house;
phrases.notes: תהלים 84:5

phrases.english: they will yet praise You, Selah."
It does not say "they praised You," but rather "they will praise You"
From here we learn resurrection of the dead from the Torah.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי: מִנַּיִין לִתְחִיַּית הַמֵּתִים מִן הַתּוֹרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another proof using the same future-tense method as רבי מאיר, from a different פסוק.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The future tense יְהַלְלוּךָ in תהלים 84:5.

steps.title: Whoever sings to ה׳ here will sing in עולם הבא
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע בן לוי teaches that whoever says שירה in this world merits saying it in עולם הבא, from the same פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהושע בן לוי also said: Anyone who says שירה in this world merits to say it in עולם הבא, as it says: 'Happy are those who dwell in Your house; they will yet praise You, סלה.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע בן לוי uses the same פסוק to teach a second lesson: there is a reward for singing praise to ה׳.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Happy are those who dwell in Your house' describes people who praise ה׳ now. 'They will yet praise You' promises they will keep praising in the future. So singing now leads to singing in עולם הבא.
steps.whatToRemember: The future-tense words in these פסוקים (יָשִׁיר, יִבְנֶה, יְהַלְלוּךָ) are read as hints to תחיית המתים. Those who sing to ה׳ now will sing again in עולם הבא.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said:
Anyone who says song to God in this world
merits and says it in the World to Come,
as it is stated: "Happy are those who dwell in Your house;
they will yet praise You, Selah."

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי: כׇּל הָאוֹמֵר שִׁירָה בְּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second teaching by the same אמורא from the same פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Whoever says שירה in this world merits saying it in עולם הבא.

steps.title: Proof of תחיית המתים from 'they will sing'
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן proves תחיית המתים from the future-tense word יְרַנֵּנוּ in ישעיהו 52:8.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חייא בר אבא said in the name of רבי יוחנן: Where do we see תחיית המתים in the תורה? From the פסוק 'Your watchmen raise their voice; together they will sing.' It does not say 'they sang' but 'they will sing.' From here we learn תחיית המתים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another future-tense proof for תחיית המתים, the same method used in the earlier steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The watchmen in the פסוק already lived in the past. If the פסוק says they 'will sing,' they must come back to life in the future to do it. This is the same future-tense method as the proofs from משה and יהושע.

phrases.english: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba said
that Rabbi Yochanan said:
From where do we know resurrection of the dead from the Torah?
As it says: "Your watchmen raise the voice;
together they will sing, etc."
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 52:8. The פסוק is from ישעיהו, yet the גמרא still calls it a source 'from the Torah.'

phrases.english: It does not say "they sang,"
but rather "they will sing" —
from here we learn resurrection of the dead from the Torah.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another future-tense proof, parallel to רבי יהושע בן לוי's proof from יהללוך.
steps.raayaObject: תחיית המתים has a source in the פסוקים

steps.title: All the prophets will sing together
steps.stepSummary: From the same פסוק, רבי יוחנן teaches that in the future all the נביאים will sing שירה in one voice.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חייא בר אבא also said in the name of רבי יוחנן: In the future all the נביאים will say שירה with one voice, as it says: 'Your watchmen raise their voice; together they will sing.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן uses the same פסוק a second time to teach a new idea about the future.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'watchmen' are read as the נביאים, and 'together' means they will all sing as one voice. This matches steps 36-37, where רבי יהושע בן לוי also used one פסוק for two teachings.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba said
that Rabbi Yochanan said:
All the prophets, every one of them, are destined
to say song in one voice,
as it says: "Your watchmen raise the voice;
together they will sing."
phrases.notes: The 'watchmen' are the prophets, and 'together' is where 'one voice' comes from.

steps.whatToRemember: One future-tense word, יְרַנֵּנוּ, teaches two things: the dead will come back to life, and all the נביאים will sing together.
steps.triggerLanguage: עֲתִידִין כׇּל הַנְּבִיאִים כּוּלָּן אוֹמְרִים שִׁירָה בְּקוֹל אֶחָד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second teaching from the same speaker and the same פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In the future all the נביאים will sing שירה together in one voice.

steps.title: Holding back Torah is like stealing an inheritance
steps.stepSummary: רב teaches that someone who refuses to teach הלכה to a student is like someone who robs him of his family inheritance.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: Anyone who holds back הלכה from a student is as if he robbed him of his ancestors' inheritance, as it says: 'משה commanded us the תורה, an inheritance of the congregation of יעקב.' The תורה has been an inheritance for all of ישראל since the six days of Creation.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic: how serious it is to refuse to teach Torah to a student.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק calls the תורה a מוֹרָשָׁה, an inheritance, belonging to the whole congregation. So every Jew owns a share in it. A teacher who holds it back is keeping from the student something that already belongs to him, which is like stealing.

keyTerms.meaning: One who holds back or withholds

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
Anyone who holds back halacha from the mouth of a student,
it is as if he robs him of his ancestors' inheritance,
as it says: "Moshe commanded us the Torah,
an inheritance of the congregation of Yaakov."
phrases.notes: דברים 33:4

phrases.english: It is an inheritance for all of Israel
from the six days of Creation.

steps.whyThisMatters: This teaches that a תורה teacher is not doing the student a favor. He is giving the student what already belongs to him.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new topic, unrelated to the proofs for תחיית המתים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Holding back הלכה from a student is like robbing him of his inheritance, because the Torah is the inheritance of all Israel.

steps.title: Even unborn babies curse one who holds back Torah
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון חסידא teaches that even fetuses curse someone who refuses to teach הלכה, and he begins quoting a פסוק from משלי.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חנא בר ביזנא said in the name of רבי שמעון חסידא: Anyone who holds back הלכה from a student, even babies in their mothers' wombs curse him, as it says: 'One who holds back בר...'
steps.whatsHappening: A second אמורא adds to the same idea with an even stronger statement. He begins quoting his proof פסוק, which continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב compared the person to a thief. רבי שמעון חסידא goes further: even the unborn are hurt, because they also have a share in the תורה, and they curse him. The proof depends on how the גמרא will read the word בָּר in the פסוק.

keyTerms.meaning: Grain (the word the גמרא will explain from the פסוק)

phrases.english: Rav Chana bar Bizna said
that Rabbi Shimon Chasida said:
Anyone who holds back halacha from the mouth of a student,
even babies in their mother's womb
curse him,
as it says: "One who holds back בר,
phrases.notes: משלי 11:26. The פסוק continues on the next amud, where the גמרא explains what בר means here.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲפִילּוּ עוּבָּרִין שֶׁבִּמְעֵי אִמָּן מְקַלְּלִין אוֹתוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on רב's teaching with a stronger statement about the same case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even unborn babies curse someone who holds back הלכה from a student.
